holding: In the wake of the above discussion, the aforesaid Civil Petitions are converted into appeals and allowed. As a consequence thereof, the impugned judgment of the learned Tribunal is set aside with the declaration that the period of services rendered by the employees before the termination of service shall be counted and included for deciding the eligibility of pensionary benefits only after re-appointment under the provisions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sacked Employees (Appointment) Act, 2012. Judge Judge

paragraphs.text: Muhammad Ali Mazhar, J: These Civil Petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the consolidated judgment dated 23.09.2024 passed by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Service Tribunal, Camp Court Abbottabad (Tribunal) in Appeals No.618 & 619/2022. CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -2 -

According to the transitory facts, the petitioners in the Civil Petitions No. 5393/2024 & 5469/2024 and respondents in the Civil Petitions No. 856-P & 857-P/2024 filed by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were appointed in the year 1995 as Theology Teachers (TT), however their services were terminated in the year 1996. After promulgation of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sacked Employees (Appointment) Act, 2012 (Act of 2012), they were reinstated in service but the back benefits were denied. After filing departmental appeal, they approached the Tribunal. Their appeals were allowed only to the extent of counting the period of service from the date of promulgation of the Act of 2012 for the payment of pensionary benefits. Both the parties are aggrieved by the consolidated impugned judgment.

The learned counsel representing the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa argued that the respondents were initially appointed in the year 1995 and terminated/sacked in 1997 but pursuant to the Act of 2012, they were re-appointed. It was further contended that under Section 5 of the Act of 2012, the appointment of a sacked employee is explicitly a fresh appointment with clear condition that the appointees shall not be entitled to any back benefits. Since the appointment was a fresh appointment hence counting of any service rendered prior to the date of fresh appointment could not be claimed even for pension, therefore, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. It was further averred that this Court in CPLA No. 468-P/2019 (judgment dated 27.03.2020), while dismissing the petition of sacked employees for seeking back benefits, held that since they had not served the department during the period they remained out of service, they are not entitled to any benefits. However, in paragraph No.6 of the said judgment, the Court observed that the petitioners shall be allowed counting of their service for the protected period for the purpose of pensionary benefits only. It was further contended by the learned counsel that the term "protected period" means the period commencing from the date of promulgation of the Act of 2012 and this position was further clarified by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Service Tribunal in its judgment dated 18.03.2021 CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -3 - passed in Service Appeal No. 572-P/2019, (Muhammad Haroon vs. Govt. of KPK), wherein the appeal was partially allowed, extending the benefit of counting service from the date of promulgation of the Act only, while rejecting the claim of back benefits from the date of initial appointment.

The learned counsel for the petitioners in CP.5393 & 5469/2024, who are also respondents in the civil petitions filed by the Government of KPK, argued that the learned Tribunal was not justified for allowing the Appeal only to the extent of counting of service from the date of promulgation of the Act of 2012 for payment of pensionary benefits. It was further contended that his clients were entitled to pensionary benefits on retirement but they were deprived of their legal right. It was further argued that the purpose of Act of 2012 was to provide relief to eligible sacked employees and Section 5 of the Act of 2012 does not specifically bar the exclusion of counting the intervening period for qualifying service for pension, therefore, it was highly unjust to exclude the intervening period from original appointment till his fresh appointment for counting the qualifying service for pension.

Heard the arguments. If we look into the minutiae of civil petitions filed vice versa against the one and common judgment of the learned Tribunal, the employees are unsatisfied for the reason that they were granted benefits for counting length of service for pension from the date of promulgation of the Act of 2012 whereas the Government of KPK relied on the niceties of Section 5 of the Act of 2012 and asserted that the appointment was rightly made with immediate effect as fresh appointment therefore even the allowance of counting service from the date of promulgation of Act of 2012 was not justified.

Seemingly, the Act of 2012 was enacted to provide relief to those sacked employees who were appointed on regular basis to a civil post in the Province of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, who possessed the prescribed qualifications and experience required for the said post but were dismissed, removed, or terminated from service on CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -4 - various grounds during the period from 1st day of November 1993 to the 30th day of November, 1996 (both days inclusive) on various grounds. According to Section 2 (g), “Sacked employee” means a person who was appointed on regular basis to a civil post in the Province of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and who possessed the prescribed qualification and experience for the said post at that time. The survey of Section 3 of the Act of 2012 prescribed the procedure of appointment of sacked employees and triggers with a non obstante clause that notwithstanding anything contained in any law or rule for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Act, all sacked employees subject to Section 7, may be appointed in their respective cadre of their concerned Department, in which they occupied civil posts before their dismissal, removal and termination from service; provided that the sacked employees shall be appointed against thirty percent of the available vacancies in the said Department; provided further that the appointment of sacked employees shall be subject to the medical fitness and verification of their character antecedents to the satisfaction of the concerned competent authority. However under Section 5 of the Act of 2012, a negative covenant has been assimilated that a sacked employee appointed under section 3, shall not be entitled to any claim of seniority, promotion or other back benefits and his appointment shall be considered as fresh appointment. [Emphasis applied]. While Section 7 of the Act of 2012 divulges the procedure for appointment which is not at issue, whereas Section 9 accentuates an overriding effect that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or rules for the time being in force, the provisions of this Act (Act of 2012) shall have overriding effect and the provisions of any other law or rules to the extent of inconsistency to this Act, shall cease to have effect.

The learned counsel appearing for the petitioners in CP.5393/2024 and CP.5469/2024 enthusiastically argued that this Court while deciding Civil Petitions No.301-P to 304-P of 2021 and some other connected cases by dint of Order dated 29.09.2025, held that the issue involved in these matters has already been dealt with by this Court vide order dated 27.03.2020 CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -5 - passed in Civil Petitions No.468 P, 469-P, 471-P and 472-P/2016 relating to other similarly placed employees of petitioner/Government and also referred to the earlier judgment on the point in issue as under:- “...The Tribunal has disallowed back benefits to the petitioners twice and it is obvious that such has been disallowed to the petitioners for the reason that they have not served the department for the said period and there is no material on record on the "basis of which relief of back benefits” could be allowed to them. There appears no illegality in the impugned judgment. Even otherwise, no substantial question of law of public importance in terms of Article 212 (3) of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 has been raised. 5. For what has been discussed above, all the listed petitions being devoid of merit stand dismissed and leave to appeal is refused. 6. It is however observed that the petitioners will be allowed counting of their service for the protected period for payment of pensionary benefits. [emphasis added]”

What we have appraised and explored that in the aforesaid matters (Civil Petitions No.301-P to 304-P of 2021), this Court held that the findings recorded in the Civil Petitions No.468 P, 469-P, 471-P and 472-P/2016), squarely covered the controversy therefore, it further held that the learned Service Tribunal, in the impugned judgments/orders, has proceeded on same reasoning, which is in full conformity with the view already taken by this Court. In the end, the civil petitions were dismissed and leave to appeal was refused. So far as other Civil Petitions No.856- P, 857-P and 5393 of 2024 which were also fixed before the Court on the same date, it was observed by the learned bench that the petitioner in Civil Petition No.5393/2024 stated that a similar petition bearing Civil Petition No.5469/2024, filed by Sher Bahadur, is pending adjudication before this Court, therefore the Court adjourned Civil Petition No.5393/2024 and directed to fix it CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -6 - with Civil Petition No.5469/2024 which we had heard on 05.03.2026 along with Civil Petitions No.856-P and 857-P/2024.

Even though this Court in Civil Petitions No.301-P to 304-P of 2021 relied upon the order of this Court dated 27.03.2020, rendered earlier in Civil Petitions No.468 P, 469-P, 471-P and 472- P/2016, reiterated and affirmed that “that the petitioners will be allowed counting of their service for the protected period for payment of pensionary benefits” but if truth be told, neither any exact or actual definition of protected period is provided in the Act of 2012 nor it has been defined essentially for all intents and purposes by the coordinate bench in the aforesaid quoted order, therefore it ought to have been glanced through for meaningful construal in the present proceedings.

Loads of emphasis was made that Section 5 of the Act of 2012 specifically excludes any claim of seniority, promotion or other back benefits and the appointment shall be considered as a fresh appointment. While denying the claim of seniority, promotion or other back benefits under this Section, no exact restrictive clause was apparently embedded in the statutory context sensu stricto by the legislature, word for word to repudiate or disregard the claim of pensionary benefits substantively for the past service rendered before sacking. The literal connotation of the stock phrase "back benefits" in fact applies to discharge the liability of retroactive/ex- post facto wages/arrears when a wrongful dismissal/termination order from service is overturned but the right of pension or its claim is treated under the law as a separate vested retirement benefit which only accrues on the eve of superannuation that cannot be unwaveringly mixed up with the payment or claim of back benefits which is in fact a compensation for the financial losses and miseries sustained by an employee during the period of termination or dismissal. When an employee is reinstated after a wrongful termination or dismissal from service, Courts/Tribunal/management may also apply the doctrine of constructive continuity which implies that the period out of job is considered continuous. CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -7 -

In fact the word “protected period” by and large describes an instantly recognizable timeframe by means of which any adversarial measure, amendment or alteration in the terms and conditions or dismissal or termination of contract or engagement is protected. Without a doubt, its crystal-clear denotation differs by context and background and the expression “protected period” does not have a standalone universal meaning but depends on the statute or legal context. It predominantly brings into play the employment laws and commercial/corporate covenants. The Cambridge Dictionary defines the word “protected” as being kept safe from harm, loss, or unwanted change; Merriam-Webster Dictionary defines it as guarded from danger, injury, or damage and Oxford Learner's Dictionary defines it as period for length or portion of time. As far as one can tell, the synonyms of the word “protected” are “safe”, “secured”, “guarded”, “sheltered” and “shielded” and in the legal taxonomy, it denotes in our view point a status or moratorium which advocates or assuages a person, right, or property from particular accountability or action to a protected class by dint of amnesty by law, rules, regulatory scheme, policy or contractual arrangements. Insofar as the use of this set phrase in the employment laws is concerned, its meaning for all intents and purposes is the time span under which the protection is accorded from discrimination, dismissal, or disadvantageous and detrimental treatment in the terms and conditions of service.

Why is the genesis of “pension” and “back benefits” distinguishable? For the reason the payment of pension is structured on different accepted wisdom and mechanisms under the relevant law and rules which only matures at the time of retirement by any means as a permanent retirement right or benefit, whereas back benefits can be regarded as compensation for active employment losses. The payment of back benefits can be denied or reduced, if it is surfaced on the record that during the period of termination and dismissal, the employee was gainfully employed elsewhere, the Court/Tribunal can reduce CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -8 - or deny the back benefits on the doctrine of "no work, no pay" but pension cannot be denied or forfeited without cover of law.

It is also pertinent to expound that payment of pension is neither dependent upon nor subject to the threshold of "gainful employment" deduction or adjustment but it operates under completely different scenario with certain pre-conditions. The purpose of pension is to provide old-age security and an economic refuge as vested constitutional right to recuperate old-age security while stepping down to the second inning which means a transition into the next phase of life in which a retired person aspires to live up to his highly anticipated imaginings or dreams and devote time to his kith and kin and friends. Ref: Muhammad Yousaf Vs. Province of Sindh (2024 SCMR 1689 = 2024 SCP 291 & Qazi Khalid Ali versus Federation of Pakistan & others (2025 SCP 305) (authored by one of us Muhammad Ali Mazhar-J). While in the case of Muhammad Ismail Memon v. Government of Sindh (PLD 2007 SC 35), it was held that the government or a department has absolutely no lawful power to withhold, seize, or arbitrarily deny pensionary or gratuity benefits. In the case of Muhammad Sharif v. Inspector General of Police (2021 SCMR 962), this Court defined the term "back benefits" specifically as current active compensation (arrears of pay, increments, and allowances upon reinstatement). The back benefits are subject to the overarching exception of gainful employment.

Likewise, the Indian Supreme Court has also laid down the jurisprudence regarding the separation of back wages and pensionary benefits. They also treated back wages as discretionary and subject to conditions like the "no work, no pay" with the proof of alternative employment but pension was treated as non- forfeitable right that accrues automatically from the continuity of service. In the case of Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyalaya (2013 10 SCC 324) and Uma Shankaran v. Union of India (2025 SC ONLINE 15560), it was held that the back wages serve the purpose of restoring the CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -9 - economic status quo of an active worker. If the employer cannot prove alternate employment, back wages are generally given, but they remain legally distinct from retirement rights. Whereas in the case of U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Anr. v. Satya Ram & Anr. (2025 INSC 339), the Court observed that physically reinstating an employee post-retirement is legally impossible and granting regular back wages beyond the retirement age is legally unjust, therefore, the Court held that instead of active back wages, the employee's dismissal period must be treated as continuous service solely to recalculate their pension, family pension from the date of superannuation onward and draw a strict line that active wages stop at the retirement cap, but pension rights continue seamlessly. In the case of Union of India & Ors. v. Tarsem Singh (2008 8 SCC 648), it was held that that if an employee delays filing a lawsuit for arrears of pay or back wages, the court can completely reject the claim due to the law of limitation (laches/delay) but a pension claim cannot be dismissed due to delay because it is a "recurring cause of action" that arises every single month.

Even in the United Kingdom Employment Rights Act 1996 (ERA 1996), back pay (arrears of wages) is strictly separated from pension rights because they are regulated under different sections of the said Act and also treated differently to cater the mitigating circumstances. Under Section 114 (2) (a) of ERA 1996, arrears of pay is regulated and an order for reinstatement requires the employer to treat the employee as if they had never been dismissed but right of pension is regulated separately under Section 114 (1), which explicitly mandates the restoration of pension rights.

The golden rule of statutory interpretation provides that the provisions should be interpreted harmoniously and congenially in line with the intention of the legislature and all the provisions should be read in unison, for the reason that the foremost stratagem of this doctrine is to preserve the effect of the statute within the precincts of law and the Constitution. The dominant object of promulgating Act of 2012 was to extinguish the unfairness and injustice to the sacked employees and on the face CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -10 - of it, the intended purpose was to set right the wrong to the employees who were afforded opportunity to join at the same place and post which brings to our mind that they had possessed the prescribed qualification, experience and competence to hold the posts but were sacked for some reasons, therefore by way of remedial edict, they were welcomed back to the jobs. On one hand the Act of 2012 is remedial but on the other hand, the Government is taking plea that the length of service prior to sacking has gone astray and they should start from scratch even for counting past service for pension which does seem the intention of the legislature if the Act of 2012 is in one piece considered in collocation.

When it is clear that the employees were made victims of sacking or scapegoat without their fault and while recognizing this injustice, the law was promulgated to undo the wrong done then there is no lawful justification to scrap or do away with the period of previous service smoothly rendered by them prior sacking without their own fault or misconduct, which should be protected for the purposes of counting in the length of service for pension eligibility, though it cannot be treated in continuity from the date of reappointment, therefore, the catchphrase “no work no pay” unequivocally applies to deny the back benefits from the date of sacking the employees till their appointment by virtue of Act of 2012 during which obviously they did not perform any work but this doctrine does not apply to the counting of period already served before sacking of employment in order to meet the deficiency in the length of service if any at the eve of retirement to disallow the pensionary benefits. While interpreting the law, it is to be read as a whole without obliterating or annihilating the other provisions to ensure the rule of harmony. The Court has to do substantial and not insubstantial justice.

The doctrine of purposive interpretation lays down a duty upon the Courts to interpret the statute keeping in mind the purposefulness for which law was legislated while adopting a result-oriented approach, rather than construing it in a restrictive CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -11 - or stringent sense and the Court must adopt the interpretation which is just, reasonable and sensible and avoid clash while construing the contradictory provisions so as to harmonize them. Under the doctrine of reading down, if the literal interpretation of any provision of law is not acceptable or leads to absurdity, then such provision may be interpreted in line with the object and purpose which the legislature had in fact in mind while enacting the law.

The straight gaze of Act of 2012 put on show that it is a beneficial law without any shadow of doubt which unambiguously amounts to one way condemning the sacking of employees and sequentially re-appointing them but not allowing the advantage of past service before sacking in which the poor employees had no role to play except a role of victim of a fortuitous event. In the case of Province of Sindh through Chief Secretary and others vs. Azhar Ali (2026 SCLR 6 = 2025 SCP 464), while speaking for the bench one of us held that the terminology “beneficial legislation” alludes to the laws, rules or regulations premeditated to vouch for the well-being of individuals and the populace. The Courts are obligated to interpret such laws, rules and regulations moderately and judiciously to make sure that the objectives of such legislation are enforced and implemented pragmatically. In order to achieve this task and safeguard the underlying principle, a dynamic, purpose oriented and liberal approach is inevitable to augment its end result. Even if a word or provision of any beneficial legislation may be interpreted in two ways that one protects and conserves the benefit but one does not or it allows diverse interpretations, then the dominant option is to pick and choose the interpretation which prospers and withstands the benefit rather than deprive it. One more important principle that cannot be lost sight of is that the philosophy of beneficial interpretation indoctrinates farther than extended connotation to the words of such beneficial provisions if such an interpretation brings into line with the legislative intent and primary objectives. It is also well-known precept of beneficial construction that it should be interpreted with CPLA.No.856-P/2024, etc -12 - proactive and dynamic approach to sync and live up to primary intended raison d'être. In order to achieve its inner self, the beneficial provision should be interpreted to shield rudimentary aspiration which is in fact an empathy of beneficial construction with generous approach and reading it with widest conceivable denotation to protect the interests of the beneficiaries of beneficial statute/provision. At times, statutes do not assimilate in every situation coherently and in such scenario, the tool of beneficial construction allows the judges to alleviate the incongruences but without varying its quintessence.

In the wake of the above discussion, the aforesaid Civil Petitions are converted into appeals and allowed. As a consequence thereof, the impugned judgment of the learned Tribunal is set aside with the declaration that the period of services rendered by the employees before the termination of service shall be counted and included for deciding the eligibility of pensionary benefits only after re-appointment under the provisions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sacked Employees (Appointment) Act, 2012.
